_note: Editor data for the tenere family (Latin tenēre, 'to hold, keep, maintain'). 26 carefully verified placements across 6 semantic regions. All etymologies explicitly confirmed to derive from Latin teneō/tenēre or prefixed forms (con-, de-, ob-, per-, re-, sub-, at-, un-). EXCLUDES: tendon (from Greek tenōn), tent (from Vulgar Latin *tenta), extend/extent (from extendō, different root). Root meaning extends from physical holding to abstract possession, maintenance, containment, and capacity. Placement format with provenance; regenerators MUST preserve by:assistant.

placements.note: One who holds or possesses land; an occupant. From Latin tenēns (holding), present participle of tenēre.
The act or right of holding something; the period of holding office. From Vulgar Latin *tenitura, from tenēre.
A holding of land; a building held by tenants. From Medieval Latin tenementum, from tenēre.
Holding firmly; persistent, stubborn. From Latin tenāx (holding fast), from tenēre.
The quality of holding firm; persistence. From Latin tenācitās, from tenāx.
To hold together; to comprise. From Latin continēre (to hold together), from con- + tenēre.
Something that contains. From contain + -er.
What is held or contained; subject matter. From Latin contentus (held in, contained), past participle of continēre.
To relate or belong to. From Latin pertinēre (to hold throughout, reach to), from per- + tenēre.
Relevant, applicable. From Latin pertinens, from pertinēre.
To keep in existence or operation; to support. From Latin manutenēre (to hold in hand), from manu (by hand) + tenēre.
The act of maintaining. From maintain + -ance.
To keep up, maintain; to support from below. From Latin sustinēre (to uphold), from sub- + tenēre.
That which sustains; nourishment. From sustain + -ance.
Capable of being sustained. From sustain + -able.
To hold or keep back; to restrain from departure. From Latin dētinēre (to hold back), from de- + tenēre.
The act of detaining; confinement. From Latin dētentiō, from dētinēre.
To keep or hold back; to continue to possess. From Latin retinēre (to hold back), from re- + tenēre.
The act of retaining; something retained. From Latin retentiō, from retinēre.
Able to retain; holding fast. From Medieval Latin retentivus, from retinēre.
To get or acquire; to secure hold of. From Latin obtinēre (to hold toward, obtain), from ob- + tenēre.
To reach or achieve; to come to hold. From Latin attinēre (to reach toward), from ad- + tenēre.
An achievement; something attained. From attain + -ment.
Capable of being held or maintained; defensible. From French tenable, from tenir (to hold), from Latin tenēre.
Not capable of being held or defended. From un- + tenable.
One who holds the place of another; a military officer. From Middle English lieutenant, from Old French lieu tenant (one holding the place), from lieu (place) + tenant (holding).
